Redis Introduction.exp: Introduction to redis and its ecosystem.

Installation: Redis can be installed via package managers, compiled from source, or run via Docker. The default configuration listens on port 6379 and stores data in memory with optional persistence to disk.

# Install on Ubuntu/Debian
sudo apt-get install redis-server

# Run via Docker
docker run --name my-redis -p 6379:6379 -d redis

# Verify installation
redis-server --version
redis-cli ping
# Output: PONG
Data Types: Redis supports Strings, Lists, Sets, Sorted Sets, Hashes, Bitmaps, HyperLogLogs, Streams, and Geospatial indexes. Each type has optimized commands for specific use cases and data access patterns.

SET stringkey "hello"
LPUSH listkey "a" "b" "c"
SADD setkey "member1" "member2"
ZADD zsetkey 1 "one" 2 "two"
HSET hashkey field1 "value1" field2 "value2"
TYPE stringkey
# Output: string
CLI: The `redis-cli` command-line interface connects to Redis servers for interactive or scripted use. It supports command execution, monitoring, slow log analysis, and server administration with built-in help.

redis-cli
127.0.0.1:6379> SET user:1 "Alice"
OK
127.0.0.1:6379> GET user:1
"Alice"
127.0.0.1:6379> INFO server
127.0.0.1:6379> MONITOR
127.0.0.1:6379> SLOWLOG GET 10

SET/GET: Strings are the most fundamental Redis data type, capable of storing text, numbers, or binary data up to 512MB. SET stores a key-value pair, GET retrieves it, and commands like `SETNX` help with distributed locks.

SET welcome "Hello Redis"
GET welcome
# Output: "Hello Redis"

SETNX lock:resource "locked"
# Output: (integer) 1 - key was set

SETEX session:token "abc123" 3600
# Sets with 1 hour TTL

MSET key1 "val1" key2 "val2"
MGET key1 key2
INCR: Redis provides atomic increment/decrement operations that are essential for counters, rate limiting, and real-time analytics. Commands like `INCR`, `DECR`, `INCRBY`, and `INCRBYFLOAT` operate on string values holding numbers.

SET counter 0
INCR counter
# Output: (integer) 1
INCRBY counter 5
# Output: (integer) 6
DECR counter
# Output: (integer) 5
GET counter
# Output: "5"

INCRBYFLOAT price 10.50
Expiry: TTL (Time To Live) automatically removes keys after a specified duration. `EXPIRE`, `TTL`, and `PERSIST` manage key lifetimes. Expiry is crucial for caching, temporary tokens, and session management.

SET cache:page "/home" 
EXPIRE cache:page 60
# Or set with expiry inline:
SETEX cache:api 300 "{\"data\": []}"

TTL cache:page
# Output: (integer) 58 - seconds remaining

PERSIST cache:page
# Remove TTL

SET key "value" EX 10 NX
# Set if not exists with 10 second expiry

LPUSH/LPOP: Lists are ordered sequences of strings, efficient for queue and stack implementations. LPUSH adds to the left, RPUSH adds to the right; LPOP and RPOP remove and return elements from either end.

LPUSH queue "task3" "task2" "task1"
# List: task1, task2, task3

RPUSH queue "task4"
# List: task1, task2, task3, task4

LPOP queue
# Output: "task1" - removes from left

LLEN queue
# Output: (integer) 3

LRANGE queue 0 -1
# Output: "task2", "task3", "task4"

BRPOP queue 0
# Blocking pop - waits indefinitely
SADD: Sets are unordered collections of unique strings. SADD adds members, SREM removes them, SMEMBERS returns all members, and SISMEMBER checks existence. Sets are ideal for tagging, deduplication, and relations.

SADD tags:post:1 "javascript" "node" "redis"
SADD tags:post:2 "python" "redis" "database"

SMEMBERS tags:post:1
# Output: "javascript", "node", "redis"

SISMEMBER tags:post:1 "redis"
# Output: (integer) 1

SCARD tags:post:1
# Output: (integer) 3 - set cardinality

SPOP tags:post:1 1
# Remove and return 1 random member
Union/Intersect: Set operations enable powerful data analysis: SUNION combines sets, SINTER finds common elements, and SDIFF finds differences. These are used for recommendations, permissions, and social features.

SUNION tags:post:1 tags:post:2
# Output: "javascript", "node", "redis", "python", "database"

SINTER tags:post:1 tags:post:2
# Output: "redis" (common tag)

SDIFF tags:post:1 tags:post:2
# Output: "javascript", "node"

SINTERSTORE common:tags tags:post:1 tags:post:2
# Store intersection in new set

HSET: Hashes store field-value pairs within a single key, ideal for representing objects. They provide memory-efficient storage with commands for individual field CRUD, bulk operations, and field counting.

HSET user:100 name "Alice" email "alice@example.com" age 30

HGET user:100 name
# Output: "Alice"

HGETALL user:100
# Output: name, Alice, email, alice@example.com, age, 30

HMSET user:101 name "Bob" email "bob@example.com"
HEXISTS user:100 age
# Output: (integer) 1

HINCRBY user:100 age 1
# Output: (integer) 31

HDEL user:100 age
ZADD: Sorted Sets associate each member with a numeric score, maintaining order by score. ZADD adds or updates members, ZRANGE retrieves by rank, and ZRANK gets position. Perfect for leaderboards and priority queues.

ZADD leaderboard 100 "Alice" 85 "Bob" 95 "Charlie"

ZRANGE leaderboard 0 -1 WITHSCORES
# Output: Bob(85), Charlie(95), Alice(100)

ZREVRANGE leaderboard 0 2 WITHSCORES
# Output: Alice(100), Charlie(95), Bob(85) - top 3

ZSCORE leaderboard "Alice"
# Output: 100

ZRANK leaderboard "Alice"
# Output: (integer) 2 - 0-indexed rank

ZINCRBY leaderboard 10 "Bob"
# Output: 95
Ranking: Sorted Sets excel at real-time leaderboards with atomic score updates, range queries, and pagination. Combined with aggregation commands like ZCOUNT and ZREMRANGEBYSCORE, they handle ranking systems efficiently.

ZREVRANGE leaderboard 0 9 WITHSCORES
# Top 10 players

ZCOUNT leaderboard 80 100
# Count players with scores between 80-100

ZREVRANK leaderboard "Alice"
# Rank from high to low

ZREMRANGEBYRANK leaderboard 0 -11
# Keep only top 10, remove rest

ZUNIONSTORE weekly 2 week:1 week:2 WEIGHTS 0.5 0.5
# Combine two weeks' scores with weighting

RDB: RDB (Redis Database) performs point-in-time snapshots at configurable intervals. It creates compact single-file backups, ideal for disaster recovery, but may lose data written between snapshots.

# redis.conf
save 900 1          # Snapshot if ≥1 key changed in 900s
save 300 10         # Snapshot if ≥10 keys changed in 300s
save 60 10000       # Snapshot if ≥10000 keys changed in 60s

# Manual snapshot
redis-cli SAVE
redis-cli BGSAVE

# RDB file location
dir /var/lib/redis
dbfilename dump.rdb
AOF: Append-Only File (AOF) logs every write operation for durability. It provides finer-grained persistence than RDB with fsync policies (every write, every second, or OS-controlled) and can be rewritten to compact.

# redis.conf
appendonly yes
appendfsync everysec     # fsync once per second
auto-aof-rewrite-percentage 100
auto-aof-rewrite-min-size 64mb

# Manual rewrite
redis-cli BGREWRITEAOF

# Check AOF status
INFO persistence
Backup/Restore: Redis backup involves copying RDB/AOF files, or using `redis-cli --rdb` for live snapshots. Restore requires stopping the server, placing the backup file correctly, and restarting. SLAVEOF enables replication-based recovery.

# Backup
redis-cli --rdb /backups/dump-$(date +%Y%m%d).rdb

# Or copy from data directory
cp /var/lib/redis/dump.rdb /backups/

# Restore
systemctl stop redis
cp /backups/dump.rdb /var/lib/redis/
chown redis:redis /var/lib/redis/dump.rdb
systemctl start redis

# Restore from AOF
redis-cli --aof /backups/appendonly.aof

Channels: Pub/Sub implements the publish-subscribe messaging pattern where publishers send messages to channels without knowledge of subscribers. SUBSCRIBE listens on channels, PUBLISH sends messages, and UNSUBSCRIBE stops listening.

# Terminal 1 - Subscriber
redis-cli
SUBSCRIBE notifications
# Waiting for messages...

# Terminal 2 - Publisher
redis-cli
PUBLISH notifications "New user registered"
PUBLISH notifications "Order #1234 shipped"

# Terminal 1 receives:
# 1) "message"
# 2) "notifications"
# 3) "New user registered"
Pattern Subscribe: PSUBSCRIBE enables subscription to channels matching a glob-style pattern. This allows listening to multiple related channels (e.g., `user:*`, `orders:*`) with a single subscription for efficient message routing.

# Subscribe to all order-related channels
PSUBSCRIBE orders:*

# Subscribe to user events
PSUBSCRIBE user:* event:*

# Publisher
PUBLISH orders:created "{id: 123, total: 99.99}"
PUBLISH orders:shipped "{id: 123, tracking: '1Z999AA10123456784'}"
PUBLISH user:registered "{id: 456, name: 'Charlie'}"

# Pattern matching: orders:* matches both orders:created and orders:shipped

PUNSUBSCRIBE orders:*
Messaging: Redis Pub/Sub is fire-and-forget with no message persistence; subscribers only receive messages sent after subscription. For reliable messaging, use Redis Streams which support consumer groups, acknowledgment, and message history.

Sentinel: Redis Sentinel provides high availability through automatic failover, monitoring, notifications, and service discovery. A Sentinel cluster monitors master/replica instances and promotes a replica when the master fails.

# sentinel.conf
sentinel monitor mymaster 127.0.0.1 6379 2
sentinel auth-pass mymaster yourpassword
sentinel down-after-milliseconds mymaster 5000
sentinel failover-timeout mymaster 60000

# Start sentinel
redis-sentinel /etc/redis/sentinel.conf

# Check status
redis-cli -p 26379 SENTINEL masters
redis-cli -p 26379 SENTINEL replicas mymaster
Cluster Mode: Redis Cluster automatically shards data across multiple nodes using hash slots (0-16383). Each node handles a subset of slots, providing horizontal scalability and automatic rebalancing when nodes are added or removed.

# Create cluster with 6 nodes (3 masters, 3 replicas)
redis-cli --cluster create \
  127.0.0.1:7000 127.0.0.1:7001 127.0.0.1:7002 \
  127.0.0.1:7003 127.0.0.1:7004 127.0.0.1:7005 \
  --cluster-replicas 1

# Connect to cluster
redis-cli -c -p 7000

# Check cluster info
CLUSTER INFO
CLUSTER NODES
CLUSTER KEYSLOT "mykey"
Sharding: Hash slots distribute keys deterministically: `HASH_SLOT = CRC16(key) mod 16384`. Client-side sharding is also possible for simpler setups, but Redis Cluster handles routing transparently with MOVED redirections.

Caching: Redis caching improves application performance by storing frequently accessed data in memory. Common patterns include cache-aside (lazy loading), write-through, and TTL-based expiry with automatic cache invalidation.
Rate Limiting: Redis enables efficient distributed rate limiting using INCR with TTL. The sliding window algorithm tracks request counts per time window, and the token bucket algorithm offers more flexible rate control.
Session Store: Redis is an ideal session store for distributed applications because of its speed, built-in TTL, and atomic operations. `connect-redis` or `ioredis-session` replace the default in-memory session store for persistence across restarts.
Queues: Redis Lists provide the foundation for lightweight job queues. `LPUSH` + `BRPOP` implement reliable FIFO queues with blocking pops. Bull and Kue are popular Node.js queue libraries built on Redis.

Redis Pub/Sub & Streams: Redis Pub/Sub enables real-time messaging with fire-and-forget semantics. Channels are created on first publish. Subscribe with SUBSCRIBE command. Redis Streams (5.0+) provide persistent, ack-based messaging with consumer groups. Stream entries are identified by IDs (timestamp-sequence). Consumer groups enable load-balanced processing with message acknowledgment. Stream features: XREAD for reading, XADD for adding, XREADGROUP for group reads, XACK for acknowledgment. Streams support blocking reads and message delivery guarantees.
